title: One Buddha or many
hook: the historical Buddha, and the many Buddhas of the Mahayana

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bodhisattva: the vow to free all beings, and two ideals each honored in its own home. Your line was both honored. Did you name the good in two different ways of living? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

Two altars. On the first, in a village temple in Sri Lanka, one seated figure: a man who walked the dusty roads of northern India, ate what was put in his bowl, grew old, fell ill, and died among his friends. On the second, in a temple in Kyoto, a golden Buddha with his hand raised, and behind him a painted sky crowded with more Buddhas than anyone could count, each with a world of its own. Same word on both altars. Buddha. Today, two pictures of who that is, and how many.
screen: `A VILLAGE ALTAR: ONE MAN.` → `A KYOTO ALTAR: A SKY OF BUDDHAS.` → `SAME WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the one. In the Pali texts, the Buddha of our age is Gotama: a teacher with a body that aches, who tells Ananda near the end that he is like an old cart held together with straps. His last words, in Rhys Davids's translation, are plain and human: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" The Theravada honors that one teacher, gone into final nibbana, and his teaching that remains. Second, the Pali texts look backward and forward. Even they are not strictly one Buddha only. A long discourse names Buddhas who came before Gotama, in ages long past, and another speaks of Metteyya, a Buddha still to come. One Buddha for an age. Many across time. Third, the many. Mahayana sutras widen the picture into space. Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light, presides over a pure land in the west, and Pure Land Buddhists call on his name. The Medicine Buddha heals in a land of lapis light. Vairocana shines at the center of the cosmos in Japanese and Chinese temples. And the Lotus Sutra adds a startling turn: the Buddha who seemed to be born, awaken and die, it says, actually awakened ages beyond measure ago, and showed a death as a teaching device so people would not grow careless. Fourth, how each holds it. For the Theravada, honoring one teacher who truly walked and truly died is the heart of devotion. For the Mahayana schools that hold it, the vast picture shows how wide awakening is. Each school explains its own altar. One and many.
screen: `GOTAMA: ONE TEACHER, AN OLD CART.` · `BUDDHAS BEFORE, METTEYYA TO COME.` · `AMITABHA, MEDICINE BUDDHA, VAIROCANA.` · `THE LOTUS SUTRA'S STARTLING TURN.` · then, large: `ONE AND MANY.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, honor both pictures. Sit and let the breath settle. First, picture the one: an old man walking slowly on a dusty road, his robe faded, his friends around him. Rest with that for a few breaths. Then let the picture open, like a camera pulling back to the night sky: light upon light, world upon world. Rest with that. You don't need to choose between them. Just let each be what it is for those who hold it. The bell holds the time.
One Buddha or many. The Buddha of our age, Gotama, honored as one teacher who lived and died; and the many Buddhas across time and space in the Mahayana. Today's word.

Your line: one and many. Today, look at one ordinary thing, a tree, a face, a cup, and see it first as the single thing it is, then as one among countless others. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor Gotama, the Buddha of this age, at temple and home shrines, while Mahayana Buddhists also honor other Buddhas, such as Amitabha in Pure Land practice and the Medicine Buddha.

fork.setup: you're at a Kyoto temple, looking at a painted sky full of Buddhas. a friend from a Sri Lankan temple asks: so which is it, one or many?
options: many; the one is just a starting point.
each school explains its own picture: one for an age, many across time and space.
fork.reveal: even the Pali texts speak of Buddhas before and after Gotama; the Mahayana widens the picture. each altar is explained in its own home.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit buddha: awakened, one who has woken up.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddha is the name of one man.
what it means: a title, awakened one; Gotama is the Buddha of our age, and there are others.
what a scholar hears: the Mahapadana Sutta's past Buddhas, Metteyya in the Cakkavatti Sutta, and the Lotus Sutra's Buddha who awakened ages beyond measure ago.

sources.work: Buddhist Suttas (Sacred Books of the East 11)

notes: Confirm the exact Rhys Davids 1881 wording of the last words (DN 16, 6.10).
The 'old cart held together with straps' image (DN 16, 2.25) is paraphrased; confirm.
DN 14 names Buddhas before Gotama and DN 26 names Metteyya to come; the count of past Buddhas is left out on purpose. Confirm.
Lotus Sutra ch. 16 paraphrase: awakened ages beyond measure ago; showed passing away as a skillful means so people would not grow careless. Confirm.
Medicine Buddha's 'land of lapis light' and Vairocana 'at the center of the cosmos in Japanese and Chinese temples' are brief descriptions; confirm.
Original note: 'awakened, one who has woken up' gives the meaning of the word, not an etymology; confirm.
Editor: stock phrase 'a detail worth hearing' replaced with 'the Pali texts look backward and forward'.
